brand.name: TECH KATTA
brand.footer: An engineering knowledge publication for distributed systems and software architecture.
brand.footerNote: Written and maintained by one engineer. Corrections welcome.

hero.title: System design, explained.
hero.description: Design interview problems on a canvas and have them judged: real traffic, crashed servers and the bill decide, and you get a score out of 100. Plus short, plain articles, built for Indian scale.
hero.figure: FIG. 01 — KAFKA: PRODUCER, BROKER, CONSUMER GROUP
hero.caption: Each key hashes to one partition, so order holds per key. Each consumer in the group owns one partition and reads it in offset order; records stay in the log after they are read.

cards.title: Concepts
cards.desc: How systems talk, store, copy and agree, the patterns that come up in every design, and specialised data such as maps, vectors and time series: what each idea means, and where it stops holding.

cards.title: Core Components
cards.desc: How load balancers, caches, queues and databases work, the named tools interviewers expect (Redis, Kafka, PostgreSQL and more), and what each one costs you when you add it to a system.

cards.title: Interview Questions
cards.desc: Common system design questions, like a URL shortener, restaurants near me or 10-minute grocery delivery, worked from requirements and rough numbers to a design you can defend.

notes.title: Quick Notes
notes.desc: Short notes on one system at a time: how it works, where it breaks, and the trade-off it makes. Each one is a few minutes' read.
items: Kafka: how a record travels from producer to consumer
Raft: leader election and log matching
Redis Cluster: hash slots and failover
Rate limiting: token bucket vs sliding window

numbers.title: The numbers behind a design.
numbers.desc: Rough latencies, and the arithmetic that turns a requirement into requests per second and terabytes. Orders of magnitude, not benchmarks.

Why data is replicated close to users.

papers.desc: The papers behind the systems you design, explained in plain words with moving diagrams: the problem each one solved, its idea, how it works, where you see it today and how to use it in an interview.

dashboard.title: Learn, then practise
dashboard.text: Concepts, Components and Interview Questions teach. Problems and the Lab are where you practise. Quick Notes are two-minute reads, and Research Papers explains the classic papers simply.

dashboard.title: Problems: practise against tests
dashboard.text: Interview problems, each with its own test suite. Design it on a canvas, Run the example tests, then Submit for a score out of 100.

dashboard.title: Worked answers
dashboard.text: Each question worked from requirements and rough numbers to a design you can defend, with the traps an interviewer looks for. It opens beside its own canvas.

dashboard.title: The building blocks
dashboard.text: Load balancers, caches, queues and databases: what each one is for and where it breaks, with figures. Concepts covers the ideas behind them.

dashboard.title: The Lab: free play
dashboard.text: Build any system from cloud parts, send traffic through it and watch what breaks. Challenges give up to three stars each.

dashboard.title: Your progress
dashboard.text: Signed in, your solved problems, scores and designs follow you to every device.

dashboard.title: That's it
dashboard.text: Press Tour any time: each page has its own. The best place to start is the first problem.

problem.title: The problem, in tabs
problem.text: Description is the brief and its example tests. Your answer, Hints, Solution and Submissions are next to it.

problem.title: Example tests
problem.text: What Run checks: traffic at the busiest hour, a failure or two, and API calls, each with the request and the response it should get. Submit adds more tests.

problem.title: Build your design
problem.text: Drag a part onto the canvas, or tap it. Join two parts by dragging from the dot on the right of one to the dot on the left of the other.

problem.title: Each part's settings
problem.text: Select a part to set it up: a name, "What it does" (a geo index, a WebSocket gateway…), its size and how many. A database also gets an engine (PostgreSQL, DynamoDB, S3…) and a Schema: the tables and keys the API calls need.

problem.title: Run
problem.text: Runs the example tests on your design. The results show what failed and why; for an API call, ▶ Watch follows the request from part to part.

problem.title: Submit
problem.text: Runs every test and grades your written answer, for a score out of 100: half for the design, half for the answer. Each submission is kept under Submissions.

problem.title: Your answer
problem.text: Write it like the interview: requirements, rough numbers, the API and the key decisions. It's graded when you Submit.

problem.title: Stuck? Hints
problem.text: One at a time, from a nudge to nearly the answer. Each one takes 3 points off.

problem.title: Solution
problem.text: The worked answer and a design that passes every test. Copy to my canvas puts it on yours to run and change; submitted unchanged, it doesn't count as solved.

problem.title: Timer and Reset
problem.text: Time yourself like the real thing, and Reset to start again from the problem's first design.

lab.title: Components
lab.text: Drag a component onto the canvas, or tap it. Each has a realistic price and limit.

lab.title: Your design
lab.text: Connect two components by dragging from the dot on the right of one to the dot on the left of the other. Click an arrow to remove it.

lab.title: Settings
lab.text: Select a component to name it, give it a job under "What it does", and set its size and count. Databases get an engine and a Schema.

lab.title: Run traffic
lab.text: Send the Clients' requests through your design on a simulated clock. Load, latency and crashes show on every component.

lab.title: $200,000 of credit
lab.text: Every design starts with virtual AWS credit, spent at its hourly cost while traffic runs.

lab.title: Challenges
lab.text: Scenarios with goals and up to three stars each, from one overloaded server to a cache that crashes at dinner.

lab.title: Your designs
lab.text: Start new designs, duplicate one with fresh credit, import your own architecture as text, or export a design as JSON.

landingLab.title: Can your design survive IND vs PAK?
landingLab.desc: On 14 October 2023, 3.5 crore people watched India play Pakistan live on one streaming app, all at the same time. Here is the real Lab with that match loaded. Add what's missing, press Score, and see if the stream holds from the toss to the last over.
landingLab.note: Peak of 3.5 crore people watching at once: ICC Men's Cricket World Cup 2023, India vs Pakistan, as reported by the broadcaster. The app here is made up. Each player fetches a 4-second chunk every 4 seconds; capacities and prices are rules of thumb.

lite.diagram: Your design, from the viewers down to your servers
lite.viewersSub: 87.5 lakh requests a second in the last over
lite.cdnSub: answers 99% near the viewers; live video
lite.lbSub: all 87.5 lakh requests a second reach it
lite.cdnHelp: Servers in cities near the viewers answer most requests, so yours see only the rest.
lite.serversHelp: Each one sends about 2,500 video chunks a second.
lite.prewarm: Start them all before the toss
lite.needCdn: Without a CDN every request lands on your servers. No farm takes 87.5 lakh requests a second: put a CDN in front.
lite.allStars: All three stars. That is how the big apps survive match night.
lite.someStars: Close. Look at which goal failed and change one thing.
lite.noStars: The stream went down. Start with the CDN.
lite.full: Build it yourself in the full Lab (on a laptop)

privacy.title: What is kept when you sign in
sections: The home page, this Privacy policy and the Terms and conditions are open to everyone. The articles, notes and the Lab ask you to sign in with Google first. Before you sign in, your Lab designs and challenge stars stay in this browser's storage and nowhere else.

When you sign in with Google: your Google account ID, name (first and last), email address, the link to your profile picture, the country you signed in from, and when you signed in. Your Lab designs and challenge stars, so they follow you to other devices. When you accepted the Terms and conditions, and whether (and when) you turned on Tech Katta updates on Facebook and Instagram. Your Google password is never seen by this site.

In a MongoDB Atlas database used only by this site. You stay signed in with a random token in a cookie that only the site's API can read; it ends when you sign out, after 30 days without a visit, or 90 days after you signed in. "Sign out on all devices" ends it everywhere at once.

When you submit a problem while signed in, the API checks your design again and keeps the result: which problem, when, whether it was accepted, the score, its cost and latency, and how many hints you opened. Not the design itself or what you wrote. These results make each problem's acceptance rate and the "cheaper than" comparison. They are deleted with your account.

To learn which articles and Lab challenges help, the site records what you do on it: pages and articles you open, how far you read, components you add, runs, scores, and signing in or out. Each browser gets a random ID kept in its own storage, not a cookie. When you're signed in, these records are linked to your account. They stay in the same database, are never shared, and are deleted after 13 months. If your browser asks sites not to track you (Global Privacy Control or Do Not Track), nothing is recorded.

Only if you turn on "Tech Katta updates on Facebook and Instagram" in the account menu (it is off until you do). Then your email, name and country are hashed and uploaded to Meta to show you Tech Katta ads. The full details are in the Terms and conditions. Turn it off any time in the same menu.
What is not done with it

No selling your data, no tracking cookies. The only outside analytics is Vercel Web Analytics, run by the company that hosts the site: it counts page views without cookies and without anything that identifies you, and it is skipped when your browser asks not to be tracked. Your email is not used to email you.

Use Delete my account in the account menu. Your account, designs, stars and the usage records linked to it are removed from the database straight away. The copy in your own browser stays until you clear it.

terms.title: Terms and conditions
sections: Tech Katta is free to use for learning system design. The articles, figures and Lab are explanations, not professional advice; the Lab's prices and numbers are estimates. Please don't overload the site, copy it wholesale, or try to break into it.

You sign in with Google, and you agree to these terms and the Privacy policy when you do. You can sign out, sign out on all devices, or delete your account at any time from the account menu. An account used to abuse the site can be closed.
Designs you make in the Lab are yours. They are kept in your account only so they show up on every device you use.

This applies only if you turn on "Tech Katta updates on Facebook and Instagram" in the account menu. It is off until you turn it on, and you can use everything on the site without it. While it is on, your email address, first and last name and country are turned into codes (SHA-256 hashes) and uploaded to Meta from time to time, so Meta can show Tech Katta ads to you on Facebook and Instagram, and to people with similar interests. Meta matches the codes against its own accounts. It does not get your designs, your stars or what you do on this site. Turn it off any time in the same menu; you are then left out of the next upload, and you can ask Meta to forget you in your Facebook or Instagram ad settings.
What the site records about how it is used, and how long it is kept, is in the Privacy policy.
If these terms change, the date at the top changes too. Anything that affects the Facebook and Instagram updates will ask you again.
